# The Weight of Numbers

Marcus is a 28-year-old financial analyst who has always found comfort in data. Numbers behave predictably. They follow rules. They can be stress-tested, modeled, and controlled. His life, until three years ago, felt much the same way — orderly, forward-moving, built on careful planning. Then his daughter nearly died, and the world stopped making sense.

Ellie was fourteen months old when she spiked a fever that wouldn't break. Marcus remembers the exact sequence: the thermometer reading 40.3, his wife Soph's voice tightening on the phone, the drive to the emergency department that took eleven minutes but felt like something outside of time. What followed was six days in the pediatric intensive care unit as Ellie fought bacterial meningitis. There were moments — and Marcus returns to these moments constantly, involuntarily — when the doctors' faces told him things their words hadn't yet. He stood in a corridor outside the PICU on the third night, alone, convinced he was about to lose her. He didn't cry. He just went very still, the way he describes it, like something inside him simply stopped.

Ellie survived. She is now four years old, healthy, loud, and obsessed with dinosaurs. By any external measure, the story has a good ending. Marcus knows this. He repeats it to himself like a mantra that has stopped working.

He cannot enter a hospital without his chest seizing. Last spring, when Soph needed a minor outpatient procedure, he sat in the car in the parking garage for forty minutes, unable to make himself go inside. He told her the traffic had been bad. He has become practiced at small deceptions — ways of hiding how much of him is still standing in that PICU corridor.

At work, Marcus functions. He is good at his job, perhaps better than ever in a technical sense, because concentration on models and spreadsheets is one of the few states in which his mind quiets. But his colleagues have noticed he is different. He declines lunch invitations. He leaves meetings early when they run long, citing calls that don't exist. The open-plan office, with its ambient noise and sudden sounds, leaves him feeling scraped thin by mid-afternoon.

At home, the difficulty is of a different texture. He watches Ellie with an intensity that exhausts him. When she coughs — even ordinarily, even once — he is already calculating: is it worse than yesterday, does she feel warm, should he call the pediatrician. His wife has gently, then less gently, named this for what it is. He knows she is right. He also cannot stop. He checks on Ellie three or four times each night, standing in the doorway of her room in the dark, watching the small rise and fall of her chest until his breathing slows enough that he can return to bed.

Sleep is its own problem. He falls asleep without difficulty and wakes at two or three in the morning with his heart already racing, the images from the PICU so vivid and present that it takes him several seconds to locate himself in the correct year. He lies still so as not to wake Soph, running through actuarial-style calculations in his head — Ellie's age, her last checkup, the statistical rarity of recurrence — as though the right numbers might finally hold the fear in place.

He describes himself as someone who used to believe that if you prepared carefully enough, you could protect the people you loved. The PICU dismantled that belief completely, and he has not been able to rebuild it. What he has instead is vigilance — constant, exhausting, and entirely his own. He carries it to work, carries it home, carries it into his daughter's room at three in the morning, and has not yet found a way to set it down.
